searchText: > Eth1 manages just fine with 20 byte addresses; 31 bytes is waaay overkill for the withdrawal commitment. I think this is dangerous! 20 byte addresses are vulnerable to collisions in `2**80` time, and bitcoin does `2**80` hashes every week I think realistically, no serious cryptographic application will be built with an 80 bit security margin this decade And collision attacks on withdrawal commitments do matter! Particularly, if you send money into a stake pool, they could (later) convince you that they can't steal your funds by showing you the opening to the withdrawal commitment that shows that it goes into a contract with known code. But if they have the ability to make two reveals with the same hash, then this guarantee breaks. IMO as part of eth2 we should honestly increase even regular addresses to 29 bytes (the remaining 3 bytes would be 1 for version number + 2 for shard ID, so the package together can still fit into one chunk) > Why is it ok to lose precision over the generated hash of the public key? A 32-byte hash with one byte truncated is just a 31-byte hash, which still has 124 bits of collision security (and 29-byte hashes would have 116 bits of collision security) If we do this it leaves addresses without checksums (at the byte level; user representation could still have checksums e.g. bech32), are we okay with this? Why would going up to 32 bytes disallow checksums? Oh I think checksums at the consensus layer are a bad idea they're definitely a user-level thing Gotcha, that makes sense.
